items.titel: Sortie de GTA VI : quels pays européens jouent et dépensent le plus dans les jeux vidéo ?
items.anriss: La fin d'une très longue attente. Treize ans après la sortie de Grand Theft Auto V, les joueurs du monde entier pourront découvrir le nouvel opus de la franchise, GTA VI, à partir du 19 novembre 2026. Le dernier-né des studios Rockstar …

absaetze.t: La fin d'une très longue attente. Treize ans après la sortie de Grand Theft Auto V, les joueurs du monde entier pourront découvrir le nouvel opus de la franchise, GTA VI, à partir du 19 novembre 2026. Le dernier-né des studios Rockstar s'annonce comme l'un des événements majeurs de l'industrie du jeu vidéo.

Le jeu aurait déjà généré un milliard de dollars de précommandes, pour un budget estimé entre 1 et 2 milliards de dollars et quelque 4 700 personnes mobilisées sur son développement. Certaines entreprises ont même accordé des congés exceptionnels à leurs salariés pour leur permettre d'y jouer, anticipant un possible pic d'absentéisme lors de sa sortie.

Le phénomène GTA VI illustre l'importance prise par le jeu vidéo dans l'industrie du divertissement. En 2025, les consommateurs ont dépensé près de 167 milliards d'euros dans les jeux vidéo à l'échelle mondiale, selon un rapport publié en octobre 2026 par l'Observatoire européen de l'audiovisuel, un organisme rattaché au Conseil de l'Europe.

Le continent européen représente environ 17 % de ce marché mondial, avec 27,7 milliards d'euros de dépenses dans les 35 territoires étudiés. Un montant qui s'élevait à seulement 14,3 milliards d'euros en 2016 et a donc presque doublé en dix ans, alors que l'inflation atteignait 33 % dans l'Union européenne sur la même période. Cette croissance a notamment été stimulée par les confinements liés à la pandémie de Covid-19.
Royaume-Uni, Allemagne, France : les trois plus grands marchés européens du jeu vidéo

Le marché européen du jeu vidéo est largement dominé par trois pays : le Royaume-Uni, l'Allemagne et la France. En 2025, les Britanniques ont consacré près de 5,93 milliards d'euros aux jeux vidéo. L'Allemagne suit de près, avec 5,67 milliards d'euros, tandis que Français y ont alloué 4,12 milliards d'euros.
L'Italie (1,90 milliard d'euros) et l'Espagne (1,57 milliard) complètent le top 5. Les Pays-Bas (1,04 milliard) et la Pologne (994 millions) occupent respectivement les sixième et septième places.
Ces différences s'expliquent en partie par la taille de la population de chaque pays. Les écarts restent importants lorsque les dépenses sont rapportées au nombre d'habitants.

Avec 86,80 euros dépensés par habitant en 2025, le Royaume-Uni arrive une nouvelle fois en tête. Il devance notamment le Danemark (69,30 euros), l'Allemagne (67,08 euros) et la Suisse (66,56 euros). La France se situe à 60,28 euros par habitant, contre 32,24 euros en Espagne et 27,17 euros en Pologne. Les montants les plus élevés sont ainsi observés principalement au nord et à l'ouest du Vieux Continent.

Les habitudes de consommation diffèrent également d'un pays à l'autre. Au Royaume-Uni et en Espagne, les consoles de salon représentent respectivement 48 % et 49 % des dépenses consacrées aux jeux vidéo. À l'inverse, le PC occupe une place particulièrement importante en Europe centrale et orientale, notamment en Pologne et en Serbie.

Le smartphone joue lui aussi un rôle majeur, notamment en Ukraine, en Estonie ou en Croatie. À l'échelle européenne, les jeux sur appareils mobiles représentent environ 40 % des dépenses en 2025, contre 37 % pour les consoles et 22 % pour les ordinateurs.
Plus d'un Européen sur deux joue, et pas seulement les jeunes
Longtemps associé à un public essentiellement masculin et adolescent, le jeu vidéo concerne désormais une grande diversité de profils.

Selon le rapport annuel de Video Games Europe, une organisation professionnelle représentant les acteurs de l'industrie du jeu vidéo en Europe, 199 millions de personnes ont joué aux jeux vidéo en 2025 dans les 16 pays européens étudiés, soit 51 % de leur population âgée de 6 à 75 ans. D'après l'étude, c'est en Autriche que le pourcentage de joueurs est le plus élevé, avec 78 % de la population de cette tranche d'âge, contre seulement 29 % en Italie.

Contrairement aux idées reçues, les joueurs sont majoritairement des adultes. 77 % d'entre eux ont 18 ans ou plus, tandis que leur âge moyen atteint 34 ans. Enfin, les femmes représentent 46 % des joueurs dans les pays étudiés.

La pratique du jeu vidéo s'est également largement diversifiée avec le développement des smartphones. Selon Video Games Europe, 82 % des joueurs interrogés utilisent notamment un smartphone ou une tablette pour jouer, contre 47 % une console et 34 % un ordinateur. Des usages qui peuvent évidemment se cumuler, un même joueur pouvant utiliser plusieurs appareils.
Plus de 120 000 emplois en Europe

Au-delà des dépenses des consommateurs, le jeu vidéo constitue également une activité économique importante en Europe. D'après Video Games Europe, le secteur employait environ 123 000 personnes dans l'Union européenne et au Royaume-Uni en 2024. Près de 8 700 studios de développement étaient recensés à travers l'Europe.

L'emploi se concentre notamment au Royaume-Uni, qui compte environ 28 500 professionnels du secteur, devant la Pologne (14 900), l'Allemagne (12 400) et la France (12 000). L'Espagne et la Suède figurent également parmi les principaux pôles européens.
Que fait l'Union européenne dans le domaine des jeux vidéo ?

Si l'industrie du jeu vidéo est largement structurée à l'échelle mondiale, l'Union européenne intervient principalement dans deux domaines : la protection des consommateurs et le soutien à la création.

Les autorités européennes renforcent leur surveillance des pratiques commerciales. En mars 2025, le réseau de coopération en matière de protection des consommateurs, coordonné par la Commission européenne, a publié des principes visant à mieux encadrer l'utilisation des monnaies virtuelles dans les jeux. L'objectif est notamment que les joueurs puissent connaître clairement le prix réel des contenus achetés avec ces monnaies, généralement acquises avec de l'argent.

Le 11 novembre 2026, la Commission européenne a présenté une proposition de règlement sur l'équité numérique (Digital Fairness Act), destinée à renforcer la protection des consommateurs face aux pratiques numériques trompeuses ou manipulatrices. Le texte vise notamment les mécanismes encourageant les dépenses excessives, les interfaces trompeuses et certaines pratiques liées aux abonnements. Il prévoit aussi de rendre plus transparent le coût des achats effectués avec des monnaies virtuelles dans les jeux vidéo et de renforcer la protection des mineurs contre certaines pratiques commerciales. Il doit encore être examiné par le Parlement européen et le Conseil de l'UE.
L'Union européenne finance également des projets de création vidéoludique à travers le programme Europe créative, et notamment son volet MEDIA.

items.titel: US criticises Ukraine's 'deep strike' campaign against Russia
items.anriss: German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the US' warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war …

absaetze.t: Published on 17 November 2026 - 23:34 GMT+1•Updated 23:42

A senior US defence official has criticised Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia, saying they had been ineffective in bringing the war to an end and arguing that, in some cases, they had likely "hardened the Russian public's resolve."
ADVERTISEMENT

"Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line," Under Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby said while speaking from NATO's headquarters in Brussels on Tuesday.

"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," he continued.
He added that support for Kyiv moving forward should focus on "enabling and advancing Ukraine's ability to hold the line of battle and where possible make gains."
Ukraine has increasingly struck targets deep inside Russian territory as the war has gone on, using its burgeoning drone technology to carry out long-range attacks.

Ukrainian forces have particularly looked to target energy infrastructure such as oil refineries and terminals, as well as military sites like air bases, as they have sought to hamper the Russian economy and hit Vladimir Putin's war machine.
US President Donald Trump has previously demanded that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were to blame for rising diesel fuel prices.
'Quite a stupid thing'
Colby's comments have drawn pushback from some European officials.

German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius called the warning "quite a stupid thing," while his British counterpart Wes Streeting said there was "no doubt" in his mind that Ukraine's long-range strikes had "helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."
The comments came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy once again urged allies to speed up deliveries of interceptor missiles.
"Ukraine needs Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from the stocks you already have right now," he told the meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels via video link.
"And I ask the United States – please, do not delay these deliveries," Zelenskyy added. He also said Ukraine needed a further 40 F-16 fighter jets to help boost its air defences.
The pleas come as Ukraine gears up for what looks set to be another brutal winter under heavy bombardment from Russian forces.
Russia has repeatedly sought to ramp up attacks on Ukraine in wartime winter periods, targeting the country's energy sector as Moscow has attempted to break its resolve.

items.titel: Russian military plane crash in Siberia kills 19
items.anriss: Russia's Defence Ministry says preliminary findings for the crash point to equipment failure.

absaetze.t: Russia’s Defence Ministry says preliminary findings on the crash point to equipment failure.
A military plane has crashed in western Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry, cited by local media.
The Antonov An-12 transport aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the city of Kemerovo, about 3,000km east of Moscow. The An-12 typically has a crew of six.
Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure.

“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by the RIA Novosti news agency.
Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had extinguished a fire. He said crews were helping to investigate the accident.
Seredyuk, in a video posted online showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when it crashed.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top criminal investigation agency, launched an inquiry into possible violations of flight safety rules, a standard practice following crashes.

The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. More than 1,000 were built, and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.
In September, a Russian Tupolev Tu-95 military aircraft crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing six crew members and injuring a seventh.

items.titel: US Fed’s Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House hearing
items.anriss: US President Donald Trump has been trying to fire Cook since August 2025.

absaetze.t: US President Donald Trump has been trying to fire Cook since August 2025.

United States Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has declined, through her lawyers, to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration of US President Donald Trump initially demanded for November 6.

Administration officials have called on Cook to appear before the committee to address allegations that she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies. Cook has not been charged with any crime.

Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook”, the letter said.

In June, the US Supreme Court blocked Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design”.

Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a November 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.

The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Department of Labor secretary.

The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire Cook if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.

Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause”, but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.

items.titel: GTA 6: What to know about the upcoming Grand Theft Auto game
items.anriss: Grand Theft Auto VI is generating huge excitement across Asia, despite restrictions on sales, censorship and the dominance of mobile gaming. While the game is not officially licensed in mainland China and faces content restrictions in …

absaetze.t: Grand Theft Auto, better known as GTA, is one of the world's most successful and controversial video game franchises. Its sixth instalment is due to launch on 19 November, with excitement spreading across Asia despite censorship, restrictions and a gaming market dominated by mobile phones.
ADVERTISEMENT

Created by Scottish studio Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games, GTA is an open-world action-adventure series. Players take on the role of criminals in fictional versions of American cities, where they can explore freely, steal cars, take part in high-speed chases and complete missions involving organised crime.
The games combine action and storytelling with satire of American society. Their depictions of violence, crime and sexual content have also made the franchise controversial.
The previous instalment, GTA V, was released in 2013 and became one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 230 million copies, according to its publisher.
Now, more than a decade later, anticipation is building for GTA VI. The new game returns players to Vice City, a fictional city inspired by Miami, Florida.

items.titel: Trump’s Demand For Steam Catapults On New Carriers Is A “Non-Starter”: Senate Armed Forces Chair
items.anriss: Senator Roger Wicker, the current chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, has said unequivocally that the idea of bringing back steam-powered catapults on U.S. Navy aircraft carriers is a “non-starter.” Earlier this year, …

absaetze.t: Senator Roger Wicker, the current chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, has said unequivocally that the idea of bringing back steam-powered catapults on U.S. Navy aircraft carriers is a “non-starter.” Earlier this year, President Donald Trump ordered the Navy to draw up plans for abandoning electromagnetic catapults and weapons elevators on the future Ford class aircraft carrier USS Doris Miller.

For years now, President Trump has railed against the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Weapons Elevators (AWE) that are core to the Ford class design. These systems have struggled with reliability and maintenance issues, but replacing them would require an immensely costly and time-consuming redesign effort. This, in turn, would risk adding to the already substantial delays in the delivery of new carriers.

The USS Gerald R. Ford is currently the only carrier in this class in operational service. In September, the Navy announced the “preliminary acceptance” of the future USS John F. Kennedy, but it has yet to be formally commissioned. The future USS Enterprise (CVN-80) is now under construction, and a contract has been awarded for the future USS Doris Miller. Work on all three of these ships is running behind schedule. There are plans to eventually acquire at least 10 members of the Ford class, including future examples to be named the USS William J. Clinton and USS George W. Bush.
“Returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that,” Wicker, a member of Trump’s Republican party from Mississippi, said while presiding over a hearing today.

He and other members of the Senate Armed Services Committee had gathered to consider the nomination of Hung Cao to become Secretary of the Navy. Cao has already been serving in this role in an acting capacity since April.

Wicker’s comments followed an exchange between Cao and Senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, regarding Trump’s directive earlier in the year on the matter of aircraft carrier catapults and weapons elevators. The President’s instructions had been contained within a larger memo outlining various naval and shipbuilding industry priorities.

“On August 13th, the President released a memorandum that included language directing the Secretary of Defense [Pete Hegseth; also referred to currently as the Secretary of War] and the Secretary of the Navy to provide a plan for replacing the current electromagnetic launch system for aircraft carriers with steam and hydraulic systems,” Kaine said in introducing his question. “I recently visited the Ford, and I went on the flight deck, and I talked to the sailors on that flight deck, many of whom had worked on carriers that both had steam and hydraulic launch systems and the EMAL system, and they were very complimentary of the EMAL system.”

The Navy’s public position historically, including during Trump’s first and second terms, has been that EMALS, as well as the Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), on Ford class carriers are worth investing in despite ongoing challenges. The service regularly touts the benefits they offer for sustained flight operations, particularly when it comes to increased sortie generation rates, compared to steam-powered systems on older Nimitz class carriers. Just in February, the service put out a press release saying a preliminary review of data collected during a new round of testing aboard the USS Gerald R. Ford further supported these viewpoints.
“Should the U.S. return to steam systems to launch aircraft off aircraft carriers?” Kaine asked Cao today.

“The whole question is how can I get, [how] I can maintain 11 carriers at this point because of the delays with EMALS and the electromagnetic elevators,” Cao said in response. “It’s delaying our carriers by seven years. We’re going to have five years where we’re going to be down to nine carriers. I’m trying to accelerate that.”
“Does that mean that you’re considering return to steam launches?” Kaine asked.

“No, no, because just the electromagnetic elevators alone, I don’t know if you know that they require certain spacing, and so you weld – what they do is they weld the elevator in place,” Cao began to say before Kaine interrupted.

“I’m not asking about the elevators. I’m asking about the launches [sic; catapults]. Based again on what the folks on the flight deck told me, the EMAL system works very, very well. And to retrofit existing carriers or change the design – you talked about in an earlier instance changing designs causes problems, and to go back to an old way of doing it is going to have an increased cost with diminished capacity,” Kaine said. “So, just because the President directed it, I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches [sic; catapults] on the Ford and before you decide to go down a path that will be more expensive and also less capable.”

It should be noted here that it has already been a matter of public record that ongoing troubles with the AWEs are continuing to contribute to delays in the delivery of new Ford class. The Navy has said previously it is working to mitigate those issues and incorporate lessons learned.

It is not entirely clear if Cao meant to voice his own opposition to returning to steam-powered catapults. He did not have a further opportunity to respond to Kaine’s questioning, and the topic did not come up again during the hearing, save for Senator Wicker’s brief additional interjection.

The comments today from Kaine and Wicker reflect already growing bipartisan pushback to Trump’s call for a return to steam and hydraulics on American carriers. The Senate Appropriations Committee drew separate attention to this matter just yesterday in an explanatory statement released along with a new draft defense spending bill for the 2027 Fiscal Year.

“The Committee notes the Department’s directed planning to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Weapons Elevators (AWE) integrated into the Ford Class Aircraft Carrier with prior-generation steam and hydraulic systems. The Committee understands that recent combat experience of Ford Class Aircraft Carriers appears to demonstrate greater sortie rates, readiness rates, and combat lethality than previous generation carriers,” the statement declared. “Further, the Committee is concerned that such a major redesign would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays. The Committee, therefore, warns against such significant programmatic shifts without substantive analysis, justification, and Congressional approval.”
The video below shows flight deck operations aboard the USS Gerald R. Ford during operations against Iran in March 2026.

“The Committee directs the Secretary of the Navy to submit to the congressional defense committees [which would include the Senate Armed Forces Committee], not later than 90 days after the enactment of this act: a report that shows comparisons of sortie generation rates between steam and electromagnetic catapults, a comparison of the manned and unmanned systems that can be launched by each type of catapult; costs of redesign for each type of air platform that was not designed to be launched under higher intensity shock and impact stresses associated with legacy catapults, comparisons of the speed and efficiency of the AWE compared to legacy weapons elevators, an estimate of the impact of such redesign on the cost and timeline for Ford Class Aircraft carrier construction and retrofitting, an analysis of the impact of such redesign on the survivability and combat effectiveness of the Ford Class Aircraft Carrier,” the statement continues. “The report shall also include separate analysis on the operational requirement changes including readiness challenges, increases in manpower needed to operate steam catapults and manpower needed for maintenance and sustainment during afloat deployments and scheduled maintenance periods.”

The explicit mention here of “unmanned systems” is worth noting. Another often cited benefit of the EMALS catapults, as well as the AAG, is that they can be more finely tuned when it comes to the forces they exert on aircraft during launch and recovery. This expands the types of platforms the systems can readily accommodate, including smaller and lighter drones, and provides additional margins of safety. For years now, the Navy has made clear that it sees the MQ-25 Stingray tanker drone and other uncrewed aircraft as central to its vision for future carrier air wings.
As TWZ previously wrote in light of Trump’s August memo:

“As mentioned, any plans now to eliminate the EMALS catapults and AWEs from the Ford class design, even just on future carriers like Doris Miller, would be a major undertaking. The core physical structure of the ship, as well as its power generation requirements and other key elements of the design, are heavily rooted in these features. All-new steam piping and the large piston systems, among other elements, would have to be installed in spaces not currently designed to accommodate them. The ship’s flight deck would have been reconfigured, as well.”

“As a result of the base design decisions, the nuclear reactor plant on the Ford class is also notably set up to generate less steam overall compared to the one on the Nimitz class, according to a past report from the Project on Government Oversight (POGO), an independent non-profit. All of this, in turn, raises additional questions about how much time and effort it would take to retrofit future Ford class carriers to use steam catapults, in particular.”

“In a time of peace, without all the threats and operational demands the United States is currently facing, or if there was any kind of surplus carrier capacity, making fundamental changes to the Ford class carrier program might very well have been a logical decision. However, all of this also comes at a time when the Navy’s operational carriers are experiencing exceptional pressure.”

Though it did not come up during Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing today, there were also reports in August that the Navy was under pressure from Trump to physically reposition the island superstructure on the Ford class on aesthetic grounds. The service has also touted the location of the island as having operational benefits as part of the overall configuration of the flight deck, which was the product of intense design studies decades ago. The President has been very vocal over the years about what he thinks warships should and should not look like. However, as with the catapults and weapons elevators, changing the position of the island now, even if limited only to future carriers in the class, would be another costly and time-consuming effort.

All of this comes amid larger continued concerns about strains on America’s naval shipbuilding capacity, which has contracted substantially since the end of the Cold War. Within this, America’s ability to produce nuclear-powered surface ships like Ford class aircraft carriers, as well as submarines, is even more limited.

This all ties into an increasingly uncertain future for another one of the Trump administration’s high-profile naval initiatives, the nuclear-powered Trump class battleship program. Earlier this month, TWZ explored the prospects for these ships going forward in light of the Democratic Party’s historic blowout of its Republican opponents.

items.titel: Hanwha transforms ship into floating multi-rocket launcher

absaetze.t: South Korean defense giant Hanwha said it successfully launched missiles from a palletizable multi-pod launcher system at sea on Sunday, demonstrating how heavy maritime strike power has shrunk to the size of shipping containers.
Hanwha Defense USA fired two Chunmoo missiles from a test range vessel operated by the Spaceport Company off the coast of Mississippi, the company announced in a Tuesday release.

The Chunmoo is a self-propelled multiple rocket launcher, designed and produced by Hanwha. Its central asset is its extreme versatility and it can fire an array of different missiles, including munitions with and without precision-guiding systems.

The U.S. Navy has been pushing for containerized weapons systems over the past year­ and in March, Admiral Daryl Caudle announced a program to shift the Navy toward modular, containerized systems that can fit onto most vessels and are easy to modify and deploy.

Addressing the fleet in April, Caudle announced a new “Containerization Plan” and emphasized that the Navy’s future will focus on adaptable technology that can integrate across multiple domains rather than platforms designed for a single purpose.

“Containerization allows us to decouple payloads from platforms. To rapidly reconfigure forces. To tailor capability to mission. To scale effects across the entire Fleet,” Caudle said in his address. “This is how we emphasize payloads over platforms in practice. It turns every platform into a potential combat node. And every payload into a scalable weapon.”
“If it fits in a container, I want it and I should be able to fight anywhere in the world with it across many, many platforms,” Caudle said.
The demand for containerized systems extends to unmanned sensors and systems, such as unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), or underwater drones.

In March, the Navy chose Anduril to design an unmanned underwater vehicle for its Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform (CAMP) Program based on the design of its Dive-XL vehicle. One of the Dive-XL’s standout features is that it fits neatly into commercial shipping containers, making it easy to transport and deploy.

According to Hanwha, the palletized launcher system it demonstrated on Sunday can be used by both crewed and uncrewed systems. This would mean that autonomous surface vessels could potentially equip multi-rocket launchers previously reserved for ground combat, effectively becoming floating launch pads for heavy firepower.
Kevin Schoonover, Hanwha Defense USA Executive Vice President, said in a statement that Hanwha is responding to the U.S. Navy’s demands to create new modern maritime strike capabilities.

“Hanwha is answering the U.S. Navy’s call to produce and field modern strike capabilities from a maritime platform. By pairing Hanwha’s flagship Chunmoo missile and its palletized platform with next generation crewed and uncrewed vessels, we can deliver capabilities for the Navy at scale and a fraction of the cost of other systems,” he said in the statement.
“The data collected during this test will help shape future distributed maritime operations and expeditionary strike capabilities for both palletized and containerized launcher concepts.”

Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “Ser III No. 5” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis, which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist, with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized.
Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale

After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tonight when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.

items.titel: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
items.anriss: At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.

absaetze.t: Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy.
November 17, 2026 — 5 min read
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.

When the “Monument Against Fascism” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque.

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.

items.titel: Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil
items.anriss: The remains of a man and a woman, both thought to have been enslaved, were in the collection of the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology for more than 150 years

absaetze.t: The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”

Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

items.titel: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks
items.anriss: Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne ’s public housing towers. In this interview , he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

absaetze.t: Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.
But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.
Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.
“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.
“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these rapprochement studies need to occur.”
Cost of relocating residents “very significant”
In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.
By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.
“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”
The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).
RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.
Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.
“There’s no public housing being rebuilt”
Formerly home to approximately 10,000 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s public housing stock.
Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.
Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.
Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.
Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.
“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.
As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.
Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.
Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.
Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.
“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.
“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.
“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”
“Public housing is foundational social infrastructure”

The issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.
“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.
“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Valley Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.
This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.
“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”
However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.
Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.
Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.
Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.
“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”
He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.
“It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”
Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.
